content:
Journalist Gio Benitez hopes to encourage viewers to effectively advocate for their heart health by going public with his coronary artery disease diagnosis.

The “Good Morning America” Sunday co-anchor and ABC News transportation correspondent, 41, said he received his diagnosis earlier this month after undergoing a calcium score test, a procedure not unlike a mammogram or a colonoscopy, which revealed calcified plaque in the arteries supplying blood to his heart.

“It shocked me because I feel totally fine. I eat right, I exercise, I do all the things ... and somehow, I had this thing,” he explained on “GMA” Tuesday. “I just want to scream it from the rooftops right now ― not for pity for me, but because I know that so many people have this silent killer inside them and they have absolutely no idea.”

He went on to note: “That is what I want everyone to know: you could feel fine, and still have this happening.”

Coronary artery disease is the most common type of heart disease. According to the National Heart, Blood and Lung Institute, almost half of adults in the U.S. have at least one of the key risk factors, which include high cholesterol and hypertension.

Despite “borderline” cholesterol numbers, Benitez says he had previously received a clean bill of health from his doctors, including a cardiologist who administered a cardiac stress test. However, lingering concerns over his family history ― including two uncles who died of heart attacks at ages 48 and 51 ― prompted him to seek further medical attention.

The next day, Benitez received his results, which showed a score of 137. Anything above 100 is considered an elevated cardiovascular risk.

In a separate interview with People, Benitez acknowledged having “panic attacks every night for about a week” after learning of his diagnosis. As “GMA” viewers can attest, the journalist is known for his active lifestyle, and frequently hosts segments that emphasize health and physical fitness.

“I couldn’t believe it. My other tests were fine, and now here it was — my worst fear, coming true,” he explained. “How could this be happening?”

Immediately following his diagnosis, Benitez began taking medication to lower his cholesterol numbers, and says he intends to increase his cardio workouts. So far, he said the results are encouraging.

“Listen, abs are going to be popping like never before,” he quipped.

A Miami native, Benitez joined ABC News in 2013, and made his official debut as a “GMA” Sunday co-anchor in 2023. He is married to entertainment journalist and podcast host Tommy DiDario.
